body_markdown:
# Jean Murray (1810–1839)

**Role:** First wife of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] — mother of his first three children. Arrived SA 1838.
**Born:** 1810 — Eskdalemuir, Dumfriesshire, Scotland
**Died:** 22 January 1839 — Emigration Depot, Adelaide, South Australia
**Buried:** Adelaide, South Australia

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Spouse** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Son** | James Telfer (1832–1845) — died aged 13 |
| **Daughter** | Esther Jane Telfer Smith (1834–1909) — went to NSW |
| **Daughter** | Elizabeth Hannah Telfer Farrow (1836–1916) — stayed at Tarlee |

## Life Summary

Jean Murray was born in 1810 at Eskdalemuir, Dumfriesshire, Scotland. She married Francis Telfer around 1831 in Scotland and bore three children — James (1832), Esther (1834), and Elizabeth (1836) — all born in the Scottish Borders and Skye regions.

The family emigrated to South Australia aboard the *Prince George*, departing London in September 1838. Jean travelled with Francis and their three young children. A fourth child, John (the baby), was born during the voyage but died at sea.

They arrived at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838 after a voyage of approximately 14 weeks. Jean died just 27 days later at the Emigration Depot in Adelaide on 22 January 1839 — likely from the combined effects of the arduous voyage and complications from childbirth.

Her death left Francis a widower with three small children under the age of 7.

title: Dinah Flavel (1821–1844) — Second Wife of Francis Telfer
body_markdown:
# Dinah Flavel (1821–1844)

**Role:** Second wife of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] — mother of his daughter Jean
**Born:** 10 June 1821 — Pytchley, Kettering Borough, Northamptonshire, England
**Died:** 20 March 1844 (aged 22) — Chain of Ponds, Adelaide Hills, South Australia
**Buried:** West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide, South Australia

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Spouse** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] (m. 4 May 1839) |
| **Daughter** | Jean Telfer (7 Aug 1840 – 15 Jul 1892) — m. A.F. Telfer |

## Life Summary

Dinah Flavel was born on 10 June 1821 at Pytchley, Northamptonshire, England — the daughter of Joseph Flavel (1797–1840) and Mary Bayes. Little is known of her childhood in England.

She married Francis Telfer on 4 May 1839 — just four months after the death of his first wife Jean Murray. The marriage took place in Adelaide, South Australia. Dinah was 18 years old; Francis was 30 with three young children from his first marriage.

Dinah gave birth to a daughter, Jean, on 7 August 1840 at Chain of Ponds in the Adelaide Hills. She died just over three years later, on 20 March 1844 at Chain of Ponds, barely 22 years old. She was buried at West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide.

Her brief life was marked by the frontier conditions of early South Australia — a young English immigrant who married a widowed Scottish farmer with young children, had a daughter, and died before reaching age 23.

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| 10 Jun 1821 | Born — Pytchley, Northamptonshire, England |
| ~1838 | Emigrated to South Australia |
| 4 May 1839 | Married [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] in Adelaide |
| 7 Aug 1840 | Daughter Jean born at Chain of Ponds, SA |
| 20 Mar 1844 | Died (aged 22) — Chain of Ponds, SA |
| | Buried — West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide |

## Family Stories

### The Flavel Family Voyage

> *According to Donald Telfer's family history (1986), Chapter 2, pp. 23–24:* Dinah travelled to South Australia aboard the *Prince George* with her parents Joseph and Mary Flavel and her six siblings, alongside the Telfer family. Her brother William Flavel later described walking barefoot from Port Misery through the sandhills, the heat running so painfully between his toes that he "had to run from one bush to another till I got clear of the sand." Dinah married Francis Telfer barely four months after the death of his first wife Jean Murray, becoming stepmother to three young children — James (7), Esther (5), and Elizabeth (4).

## Sources

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 21–25 — extract via vision_analyze 19 June 2026

title: James Telfer (1832–1845) — The Lost Boy
body_markdown:
# James Telfer (1832–1845)

**Role:** Eldest son of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] and Jean Murray — vanished at age 13
**Born:** 1832 — Scotland
**Disappeared:** July 1844 (aged 13) — Chain of Ponds area, South Australia
**Declared dead:** ~1845 (presumed)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Mother** | [[Jean Murray (1810–1839)]] |
| **Stepmother (1)** | [[Dinah Flavel (1821–1844)]] |
| **Stepmother (2)** | [[Margaret Wright Telfer (?–1892)]] |
| **Sister** | Esther Jane Telfer (1834–1909) — m. John Smith |
| **Sister** | Elizabeth Hannah Telfer (1836–1916) — m. Charles Farrow |
| **Half-sister** | Jean Telfer (1840–1892) |

## Life Summary

James was born in Scotland in 1832, the eldest of Francis and Jean's kids. He made the voyage on the *Prince George* with his parents and two younger sisters, docking at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. His mother died just 27 days later — leaving Francis with three kids under 7.

James grew up in the Adelaide Hills frontier on his father's farm near Chain of Ponds. By 13 he was working as a shepherd on the family sheep station.

## Family Story — The Disappearance of James Telfer

In July 1844, during a week of heavy rain, James left the sheep station on the River Torrens near Chain of Ponds to round up stray sheep. He never came home.

Francis raised the alarm that night. Neighbours searched for days but the creeks were flooded and rain hadn't let up. Nothing was found. The general feeling was the flood took him. People figured when waters dropped, his remains would turn up in the riverbed or the Reedbeds. They didn't.

The *South Australian Register* printed this on 10 July 1844 (p.3):

> **"BOY MISSING** — On Tuesday last, during the heavy rain then falling, a youth named Telfer, thirteen years old, left his fathers sheep station on the River Torrens, near Chain of Ponds, to recover some stray sheep, but up to Saturday last had not been heard of. The surrounding country has been searched, but no trace of the wanderer has been found: and from the late inclemency of the weather, there is too much reason to believe that he has perished."

Family stories over the years threw up different theories — killed by aborigines, step-mother troubles, ran away. The most detailed version came from William Flavel: one morning someone walked twelve miles to tell Francis, who rounded up every man in the district. They searched for days, then got the police from Adelaide. Nothing.

Then around 1877 — 33 years later — a newspaper article reported that recent floods had washed away logs and debris lodged against a tree in the river near Adelaide. Amongst the debris was a human skeleton. Police took charge. A doctor said the bones were a boy about 13, probably there for more than 20 years.

Whether Francis ever learned his son had been found is unknown.

Tragically, James was the fourth family member Francis had lost in six years — wife Jean (1839), infant son John (died at sea 1838), second wife Dinah (1844), and now his eldest boy.

*(Based on Donald Telfer, From the Borders to the Bush, pp.25–27, and the SA Register, 10 Jul 1844)*

## Sources

- Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 25–27 — story reference, not verbatim
- South Australian Register, 10 July 1844, Page 3, Col. A — public domain newspaper quote

title: Esther Jane Telfer (1834–1909) — From Scotland to Nyngan
body_markdown:
# Esther Jane Telfer (1834–1909)

**Role:** Daughter of Francis Telfer — matriarch of the Smith line
**Born:** 21 May 1834 — Isle of Skye, Scotland
**Died:** March 1909 (aged 75) — Nyngan, New South Wales
**Buried:** Nyngan Cemetery (Church of England section)
**Spouse:** John Smith (~1827 – 5 May 1895)
**Ship:** *Prince George* — arrived Port Adelaide 26 December 1838 (aged 4)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Mother** | Jean Murray (1810–1839) |
| **Husband** | John Smith |

### Children

| Child | Born | Died | Married |
|-------|------|------|---------|
| Jane Sophie Smith | South Australia | Apr 1913 (aged 47) | Benjamin Harper |
| Margaret Dougal Smith | Burra, S.A. | 30 Oct 1961 (aged ~93) | Thomas Parkins |
| Esther Telfer Smith | 27 Sep 1870, Tungkillo S.A. | 5 May 1896 (aged 25) | Thomas Henry Kent |
| John James "Jack" Smith | 1871, Tungkillo S.A. | — | Idona Caston Murray |
| Francis Telfer "Frank" Smith | 14 Feb 1874, Mt Gambier S.A. | 9 Jul 1945, Nyngan | Ellie Forbes, Catherine Gibson |
| Elizabeth Anne Smith | 1878, Millicent S.A. | — | — |

## Life Summary

### Early Life

Esther was born on the Isle of Skye to Francis Telfer and Jean Murray — the second of their three children. When she was four, the family sailed for South Australia aboard the *Prince George*, arriving at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. Her mother Jean died at the Emigration Depot barely a month after landing.

Esther grew up at Chain of Ponds in the Adelaide Hills, then Kersbrook, where her father Francis farmed and helped establish the Church of Christ.

### Marriage to John Smith

On **16 November 1863** at the **Wesleyan Parsonage, Kapunda**, Esther married **John Smith** — a man born in Copenhagen, Denmark in 1830, son of a Scottish Sea Captain and a Danish mother. John had bought a block of land on Gunningbah Creek, north of Nyngan, running sheep. Together they had six children.

### The Move to Victoria

The family set out for Victoria, but Esther, pregnant with her sixth child, found the journey by horse-drawn wagon with steel-rimmed wheels on dirt roads too much. She stayed in Millicent (South East) until after Elizabeth Anne was born in 1878, while John and some of the children pushed on to Natimuk, Victoria to set up a new home.

Their new home, called **"Ebenezer"**, was a pug-and-thatch construction at Sherwood Dam near Mount Arapiles. The children attended Arapiles School.

### The Trek to Nyngan

Towards the end of the 1880s, the two oldest boys — John James and Francis Telfer — rode pushbikes some 600 miles into the outback to Nyngan to scout land. They came back with glowing reports.

The family sold their Natimuk farm to the Lange family and set out on a weeks-long trek to Nyngan in a wagon drawn by four draught horses. Their diet: damper cooked in camp ovens, corned meat, and whatever rabbits and birds they caught along the way. Water bags hung from the side of the wagon in the shade to keep cool.

John bought the block on Gunningbah Creek and ran sheep there until his death on 5 May 1895.

### Later Life

After John died, Esther moved into Nyngan township — a brick home in Wambiana Street. She was described as a tiny person, just five feet tall, a devoted mother and grandmother, and a loyal church supporter.

Her home was still standing in good condition as of 1984.

She died in March 1909, aged 75, and was buried with her husband in Nyngan Cemetery.

## Family Stories

### The Bike Scouts

In the late 1880s, Esther's two boys — John James (about 17) and Francis Telfer (about 15) — rode pushbikes nearly 600 miles from Natimuk, Victoria into the wilds of outback New South Wales to scout land. They returned full of talk about Nyngan and the land opening up. It was their report that convinced the family to pull up roots and make the long trek north.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.39–40)*

### Essie Ray — Esther's Granddaughter

Essie (Esther Jane Harper, granddaughter through Jane Sophie) grew up walking 2.5 miles to school, milking a cow before she left. At about age 11, her family moved from Miram, Victoria to Mullengudgery, NSW. Her mother died of pneumonia about three years later. At just 14, she kept house for six children in a big house with board floors she scrubbed weekly on hands and knees, made butter, did all the cooking, and looked after the lot.

Her brother rode a bike 27 miles into Nyngan to get the doctor — there were no telephones. Too late.

She later married Alex Stevenson (a "nice chap"), had two children. Alex died in his 30th year. She supported herself by dressmaking. Married second to Robert Ray, a widower with two grown daughters. Learned to drive a truck to take fruit from their orchard to the railway.

She celebrated her 90th birthday on 4 January 1989 and still attended Presbyterian Church and Guild, and had a life membership badge from the Orange Show.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.40–41)*

### The Promise to a Dying Sister

Esther's namesake daughter, Esther Telfer Smith, married a Wesleyan minister named Thomas Henry Kent. Thomas died of consumption on 17 December 1895 — just eight months after their wedding. The younger Esther followed him to the grave five months later, also from consumption, on 5 May 1896.

On her deathbed, she asked her sister Margaret: *"If you ever go to Melbourne, will you visit Thomas's grave?"*

Forty-six years later, Margaret — then a widow herself — visited her daughter Ruby and son-in-law Roy Pearce at Bendigo. Roy drove her to Melbourne, and she fulfilled her sister's dying wish.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.44–45)*

### The Eudora Merino Stud

Esther's youngest son, Francis Telfer Smith, drew a block at Mullengudgery (27 miles out of Nyngan) in 1898 and named it **"Eudora"**. He built a large weatherboard home surrounded by shade trees, a big garden with stone fruits and citrus, and a tennis court. He established the Eudora Merino Stud and took sheep to the Royal Sydney Show.

He was a keen pushbike rider in his youth — once rode from Eudora all the way to Mount Gambier with two friends. He also owned racehorses: "Pearl George" and "Pharalie" were sold and shipped to India during WWI.

His daughter Ena recalled: no refrigeration — a charcoal safe with a troublesome door and a green frog living in the water tray on top. Canvas water bags hanging on the verandah. Round galvanised tubs for bathing — knees under chin or legs over the side. Their first car was a T Model Ford; summer nights with the hood down, chugging along at about 20 mph.

When the 1955 flood hit the Bogon River, the Dubbo Aero Club dropped food parcels that burst hitting the water. The family fished tins out of two feet of floodwater — labels lost. They opened cat food for lunch once without realising.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.47–57)*

### Jack Smith Saves Melrose

Esther's oldest son John James "Jack" Smith lived at "Brooklands" on Duck Creek and ran a Merino stud. When his sister Margaret Parkins' husband Thomas was killed in a sulky accident in 1917, Margaret struggled to keep their property "Melrose" going. Her son Dougal hit bad seasons and couldn't make ends meet. The bank threatened to foreclose.

Jack walked into the bank, threw his cheque book on the manager's desk, and said: *"Take what you want out of that, but don't you dare put Margaret Parkins — a widow — out of Melrose."*

Melrose stayed in the Parkins family for 61 years.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.44, 46)*

## Sources

- **Note:** WikiTree lists husband as "Hans Hansen (Jorgenson) Smith" — "Hans" is the Danish equivalent of "John". The book confirms he was born in Copenhagen, son of a Scottish Sea Captain and Danish mother, consistent with anglicising his name to John Smith in Australia.
- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 36–57 — extract via OCR and vision analysis 19 June 2026
- FindAGrave: [Esther Jane Smith (1834–1909)](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/252916720) — Nyngan Cemetery
- WikiTree: [Esther Jane Telfer (Smith) (1834–1909)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Telfer-591)

title: Elizabeth Hannah Telfer (1836–1916) — Matriarch of Hope Farm
body_markdown:
# Elizabeth Hannah Telfer (1836–1916)

**Role:** Second daughter of Francis Telfer — matriarch of the Farrow line at Hope Farm, Tarlee
**Born:** 7 June 1836 — Dumfriesshire, Scotland
**Died:** 8 October 1916 (aged 80) — Tarlee, South Australia
**Buried:** Tarlee Cemetery (beside husband)
**Spouse:** Charles Farrow (~1836 – Dec 1884) — m. 28 March 1856
**Ship:** *Prince George* — arrived Port Adelaide 26 December 1838 (aged 2)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Mother** | Jean Murray (1810–1839) |
|| **Husband** | Charles Farrow (~1836 – Dec 1884) ||
| **Sister** | [[Esther Jane Telfer (1834–1909)]] |

### Children (all born at Hope Farm, Tarlee)

| Child | Spouse |
|-------|--------|
| Jane Murray Farrow | Alfred Stribling |
| Esther "Ettie" Farrow | Richard Pelling Latter |
| Elizabeth Telfer Farrow | Thomas Holloway |
| Joseph Francis Farrow | Annie Louise Downton |
| Charles Farrow Jr | Ethel Mary Sambell |
| Amy Farrow | Sidney Stribling |
| John James Telfer Farrow | Emily Smithers |
| George Hope Farrow | Caroline Stanton |
| Mary Bayes Farrow | Alfred Edward Lillecrapp |
| Eva Agnes Farrow | Walter Hookings |

## Life Summary

Elizabeth was born in Dumfriesshire, Scotland to Francis Telfer and Jean Murray. She was just two years old when the family sailed for South Australia on the *Prince George*, arriving at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. Her mother Jean died at the Emigration Depot barely a month later.

She grew up at Chain of Ponds and Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills. On 28 March 1856, aged 19, she married **Charles Farrow** at her family's home on Section 6146, Parra Wirra. The ceremony was performed by Rev. William Vercoe, witnessed by A.B. Murray and P.M. Murray — Elizabeth's uncles.

They settled at **Hope Farm**, Finniss Point, near Tarlee — 152 acres Charles had bought from John Ridley for £319/4. Charles had walked from Kersbrook to Tarlee weekly carrying food, then built a small stone cottage by hand with an axe.

Elizabeth was described as a "very kind and most gracious lady, always quick to help anyone in need." She was a foundation member of Tarlee Baptist Church. After Charles died of pneumonia in 1884, she ran the farm with her sons for over three decades.

Her father Francis Telfer came to stay with Elizabeth at Hope Farm before his death on 2 September 1895, and was buried at Tarlee Cemetery.

She died on 8 October 1916, aged 80, and was buried beside Charles.

## Family Stories

### The Bull at Tuppeny Well

Not long after Charles bought Hope Farm, he was walking there on a hot Monday. About two miles south of Tarlee on the eastern side of the main road was a shallow well called "Tuppeny Well" — the owner charged tuppence to water bullocks and horses. An irate bull came up for a drink. There were no trees nearby, so Charles climbed a six-to-seven-foot whip post used to draw water and sat there until dark when the bull wandered off. Then he walked the remaining six miles home.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.59)*

### The Fire of 1865

On Saturday, 25 March 1865, fire destroyed the Farrow cottage. The roof was gone, part of the front wall collapsed, and most of their belongings. Amos Flavel's diary recorded it: *"Mr Farrow helping put out the fire but the roof was destroyed & part of the front wall of the house & a very great deal of other things."*

Charles rebuilt — a larger house with a galvanized iron roof and guttering. It was still standing when the Tarlee reunion was held on 2 December 1984.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.59–60; Amos Flavel Diary, 25 Mar 1865)*

### The Water Walk

During a long dry summer, the rainwater tanks at Hope Farm ran dry. With three small girls to care for, Elizabeth would tie baby Elizabeth Telfer Farrow to the kitchen table leg with a leather strap, take Jane (age 5) and Esther (age 3), and walk 14 miles to Deep Creek to carry back water for the family's daily washing.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.61)*

### Charles's Last Night

On 2 December 1884, Charles returned home from his rounds travelling the district with his draught stallion for mating. He was wet through from heavy showers. He told his son Charles Junior to put the horses away: *"I am feeling very ill."*

That night he became much worse. Elizabeth woke Charles Junior to ride to Kapunda for the doctor. The doctor arrived around 4am and promised to return that afternoon. Charles Farrow died just before the doctor got back — pneumonia, in the days before penicillin.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.62)*

### Tarlee Baptist Church

In June 1868, the Farrow home hosted the founding meeting of Tarlee Baptist Church. Charles was appointed Deacon and lay preacher, serving for over 16 years. The Minute Book recorded after his death:

> *"This Church deeply mourns the death of Brother Farrow Senior and desires to record the Church's appreciation of his devoted labours in the cause of Christ among us."*

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.63)*

### Ashley Cooper's 80th Birthday

Ashley Cooper, born in 1908, was the grandson of Elizabeth's daughter Esther Farrow. He worked for the Adelaide Steamship Company as an auditor, travelled to coastal shipping centres, and during WWII was transferred to Perth to oversee merchant ships used as troop carriers. He travelled extensively in the Flinders Ranges — Parachilna, Beltana, Moralana — and wrote a book on the history of Beltana. He suffered a stroke but kept typing one-fingered. He celebrated his 80th birthday in March 1988.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.68)*

## Sources

- **Note:** The book header lists Charles Farrow as (1837–1876) and the family tree as (1828–1876), but the narrative clearly states he died in December 1884 — 32 years before Elizabeth's 1916 death. The detailed story (Dec 1884, pneumonia) is taken as accurate over the header dates. Born ~1836 based on being age 19 when buying the farm in Nov 1855.
- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 58–75 — extract via OCR 19 June 2026
- WikiTree: [Elizabeth Hannah Telfer (1836–1916)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Telfer-590)

body_markdown:
# Frederick Parker (~1838–1928)

**Role:** Second husband of Jean Telfer
**Died:** 1928 — Wildes Meadow, New South Wales
**Buried:** Bowral Cemetery, NSW

Frederick Parker, son of George Parker, married Jean (who had by then adopted the name Jane) on Christmas Day 1871 at Kapunda. They lived at Finniss Point before moving to the far north of South Australia around Hawker and Oraparinna.

After Jane died in 1892 from heart disease, Frederick later went to live with his elder daughter Margaret and son-in-law Edward Liebich at Wildes Meadow, New South Wales. He died in 1928 and is buried in Bowral Cemetery.

title: Richard Paynter — Family & Biography
body_markdown:
# Richard Paynter (1838–1869)

**Role:** First husband of Jean Telfer
**Born:** ~1838 — Cornwall, England
**Died:** 7 February 1869 (aged 30) — St. Kitts Creek, pleurisy
**Buried:** Kapunda area

Richard Paynter was born in Cornwall, England, the son of Richard Paynter of Calstock. He emigrated to South Australia where he worked as a labourer at Chain of Ponds.

He married Jean Telfer on 12 September 1859 at the Chain of Ponds Parsonage, solemnised by John Kither and witnessed by her father Francis Telfer and Henry Whiting. Jean was several months pregnant at the time.

After their first child Thomas was born, the family moved to Koppio near Port Lincoln where Richard worked as a shepherd for Jean's cousin James Telfer. They later returned to the Chain of Ponds area and then to St. Kitts between Kapunda and Truro, where Richard became the local school teacher — a change brought on by his failing health.

Richard died of pleurisy at the age of 30, leaving a widow and five children unprovided for.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — Chapter on Jean/Jane Telfer
roles: First husband of Jean Telfer

title: Jean (Jane) Telfer (1840–1892) — Daughter of Francis Telfer
body_markdown:
# Jean (Jane) Telfer (1840–1892)

Third daughter of **[[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]]** and **Jean Murray**. After her mother's death, she was step-raised by **Dinah Flavel** (her father's second wife).

## Vital Information

- **Born:** 7 August 1840
- **Birth name:** Jean Telfer (marriage certificate gives name as "Jane")
- **Died:** 15 July 1892, Queens Own Town (Finniss Point), South Australia — heart disease
- **Buried:** Strathalbyn Cemetery, South Australia

## Marriage (1): Richard Paynter (1838–1869)

- **Marriage date/location:** Solemnized by John Kither (Officiating Minister) at Chain of Ponds Parsonage. Witnessed by her father Francis Telfer and Henry Whiting of Chain of Ponds. Jean was several months pregnant at the time.

- Born 1888. Married (1) Sarah Jane Barbour, (2) Lily Olive Rowe. Worked for railways. Died 1 Jul 1946, aged 58.

##### 1d. Ethel Emily Elizabeth Paynter
- Born 1891, Arden Vale. Married (1) Frank Smith (railway worker — d. 1932), (2) David George Flavel (railway ganger). Died 19 May 1932, Peterborough.

##### 1e. Dinah Alice Mary Paynter
- Born 27 Sep 1894, Arden Vale. Married William Mundy (railway employee). Died 27 May 1963.

##### 1f. Agnes Letitia May Rose Paynter
- Born 1896, Arden Vale. Married George Hucks (railway worker). Died 28 May 1952, buried Loxton.

- Born 8 Aug 1900, Quorn nursing home. Married John Hunter Rankin (of Koolunga, son of Scottish migrants Angus and Jane Rankin) in 1918. Died 8 Jul 1988, Port Augusta.

- Born 31 Dec 1903, Arden Vale. Married Florence Catherine Donovan. Died 16 Sep 1940, aged 36.

##### 1i. Helena Florence Daisy Paynter
- Born 19 Aug 1906, Arden Vale. Married Harry Richmond Hill (northern station hand). Lived in Terowie, later Gawler.

#### 2. MARY JANE PAYNTER
- **Born:** 30 June 1861, Koppio (near Port Lincoln)
- **Married:** John Watson, 1 March 1882. Ceremony by Rev. H. Chapman (first Wesleyan Minister of Hawker), witnessed by Mrs Anne Mapleton and John Telfer (Mary's uncle).
- **John Watson:** Grandfather Charles Watson was a convict on "Asia II" (1827, Tasmania). John was a "lime burner" of Arkaba.
- **Lived:** Willow Plains (share-farmed land owned by John Telfer). Moved to Olinda, Victoria in 1910.
- **John died:** 10 September 1929

Gilbert Melville Telfer (the book records his given names as Gilbert Melville, not Melvin McLeod — he was known as "Mel") was born in 1911, the third child of Mark Telfer (1877–1946) and Julia Matilda Seebohm (1876–1939) of Tantanoola, South Australia.

He married Jessie Allan and they had three children — Beth, who married Clive Lipscombe; Ian, who married Sally Taylor; and Allan, who married Christine Marshall.

Mel was a good footballer, playing at centre wing and proving formidable as a fast player and a good ball handler. He was an opening batsman for the Tantanoola Cricket team and made many centuries. He was a most useful member of the team and excelled as the wicket keeper. When his eyesight no longer permitted him to play football and cricket, Mel played bowls, both indoor and outdoor, and proved to be an excellent player.

Like his father and brothers, he was interested in local affairs and was a Life Member of the Tantanoola Pastoral, Agricultural and Horticultural Society.

In his father's obituary, he was listed as "Mel Telfer, Tantanoola".

## Life Summary

Francis Telfer was born on 2 February 1809 at Blackburn Foot (the old Black Burn fort) in Liddesdale, Roxburghshire, Scotland — the seventh of eight children born to James Telfer and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton. He grew up in the Castleton region of the Scottish Borders.

### The Voyage

Francis emigrated to South Australia aboard the *Prince George*, departing London in September 1838 and arriving at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. He travelled with his first wife Jean Murray and their three young children: James (6), Esther (4), and Elizabeth (2). A fourth child, John (the baby), died during the voyage.

### Three Marriages

Francis outlived his first two wives. Jean Murray died shortly after arrival at the Emigration Depot in Adelaide on 22 January 1839 — barely a month after landing. Her infant son John had died during the voyage.

Within months, Francis married **Dinah Flavel** (a young English immigrant from Northamptonshire) on 4 May 1839. They had one daughter, Jean (born at Chain of Ponds, 1840). Dinah died on 20 March 1844 at Chain of Ponds, aged only 22, and was buried at West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide.

On 27 March 1845, Francis married **Margaret Wright**, with whom he had three more children: John (the main line ancestor), Margaret Dougal, and George Wright. Margaret Wright brought stability to the household and outlived Francis, dying in 1892.

### Later Life

Francis farmed at Chain of Ponds and Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills before settling at **Hope Farm, Tarlee**, in the Clare Valley region. He became a respected local identity. By the time of his death at age 86, he had established the Telfer name across South Australia.

His obituary in *The Border Watch* (18 September 1895) recorded:
> "He leaves two sons — Mr. John Telfer, of Hawker, and Mr. G. W. Telfer, Willaston — and three daughters — Mrs. Farrow, of Hope Farm, Mrs. Smith, of Canouba, New South Wales, and Mrs. A. F. Telfer, of Edgerston, Tantanoola."

Francis died at Hope Farm, Tarlee on 2 September 1895. A memorial headstone was erected by the Telfer Family History Association in 1999, commemorating his three wives and his place as the founder of the Australian Telfer line.

## Family Stories

### The Lost Boy — James Telfer (1832–1845)

Francis's eldest son James, aged 13, disappeared while bringing in stray sheep during heavy rain in July 1844 near Chain of Ponds. Neighbours, police — they scoured the flooded countryside for days. Nothing. The *South Australian Register* ran a notice on 10 Jul 1844 asking for information. James was never seen alive again.

Around 1877, floodwaters receded near Adelaide and a human skeleton was found lodged against a tree in the river. A doctor said it was a boy about 13, probably there 20+ years. Whether Francis ever found out is unknown.

It was the fourth family member Francis lost in six years: infant John (died at sea, 1838), wife Jean (1839), wife Dinah (1844), and his eldest son James.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.25–27; SA Register, 10 Jul 1844)*

### The Flavel Family and the Voyage of the *Prince George*

Francis sailed to South Australia on the *Prince George* alongside the Flavel family — Joseph and Mary Flavel and their seven kids. The Flavels became lifelong friends. William Flavel remembered arriving at Port Misery on 26 Dec 1838 and walking barefoot across the sandhills, where the summer sand was so hot he "had to run from one bush to another till I got clear of the sand." The Flavel baby, John Telfer, died during the voyage and was buried at sea.

The *Prince George* was a 482-ton, 118-foot, 3-masted barque under Captain Young. Francis applied for emigration on 9 August 1838, had just 26 days to prepare, and sailed from London on 4 September 1838.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.22–24)*

### Francis and the Kersbrook Church of Christ

Francis was an intensely religious man. He regularly walked 22 miles from Kersbrook to Adelaide for the "Scotch Kirk" (Gouger Street United Presbyterian Church). In 1863, he became a founding trustee of the Kersbrook Church of Christ Chapel and served as Sunday School Superintendent. He was described as "the pastor's right hand" alongside John McMillan.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.27–31)*

### Francis's Last Letter — To Jane Murray Perry

About a month before Francis died at age 86, he wrote a letter to his granddaughter Jane Murray Perry (the daughter of his daughter Jean/Jane Telfer). The letter was written at Hope Farm, Tarlee and spoke of his life, his belief in God, and his hopes for his family. It is one of the few surviving documents in Francis's own hand — a direct connection to the man who founded the Australian Telfer line.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.33)*

### The House at Macoota

Francis's stone house at Section 6146, Kersbrook had walls 15 inches thick of local stone. Originally shingle-roofed (still preserved under later iron), it had a central passage, three bedrooms off the south side, a kitchen/dining room and drawing room with large fireplaces on the north, and a well about 50 yards from the back door. The land was so thick with wattle and banksia scrub you couldn't walk through it when first taken up.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.31–33)*

### Margaret Wright and the Stirling Castle Legend

Family legend had it that Francis's third wife Margaret Wright was "born in Stirling Castle" — though which bit of the castle was left for debate. Problem is, the last king to actually live there was James VI (1567–1625), long before Margaret was born. Colourful story, suspect geography.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.27)*

Susan Burton married Robert Telfer and settled in the Mount Gambier district of South Australia. Her husband Robert worked as stock manager at Moorak, one of the large pastoral estates near Mount Gambier. When Dr. Browne subdivided the Woodlands estate, Robert purchased a farm there and the family moved to that property at Yahl, near Mount Gambier.

## Life Summary

Margaret Wright was the **third wife** of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]]. She married him in South Australia after the deaths of his first wife Jean Murray (d. 1839) and second wife Dinah Flavel.

She was the mother of:
- **[[John Telfer (1847–1929)]]** — Mark's great-great-grandfather

Margaret Wright died on **13 September 1892** at Kersbrook and is buried at Kersbrook Cemetery (General, Section B, Row 1, Plot B13). Her death came about **three years before Francis**, which prompted his eventual move from the farm at Kersbrook to live with his son at Gawler.

## About the Three Wives of Francis Telfer

Francis Telfer married three times — an unusual number that sometimes causes confusion in genealogical records:

1. **Jean Murray** — married in Scotland, mother of James (1832), Esther Jane (1834), Elizabeth (1836). Jean died 22 Jan 1839, shortly after arrival in SA.
2. **Dinah Flavel** — second wife in South Australia
3. **Margaret Wright** — third wife and mother of John and the younger children

Some trees simply list "Margaret Telfer" as Francis's wife without specifying which marriage, leading to contradictions between sources.

## Family Stories

### The Stirling Castle Legend

> *According to Donald Telfer's family history (1986), Chapter 2, p. 27:* Family tradition held that Margaret Wright was "born in Stirling Castle." Which room — the main bedchamber, a guest room, or the servants' quarters — was left for speculation. The last reigning monarch to live at Stirling Castle was James VI (1567–1625), so the story may refer to her family's residence within the castle precincts rather than the royal apartments.

## Life Story

John Telfer was born in **Adelaide, South Australia** on **28 May 1847** — the eldest surviving son of Scottish immigrant [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)|Francis Telfer]] and his third wife Margaret Wright. He grew up on the family farm at Chain of Ponds and Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills.

On **22 September 1874**, he married **Caroline Amelia Masters** at the Baptist Chapel, Tarlee. The marriage was announced in the South Australian Register. Caroline had immigrated from England as a young child with her family aboard the *Templar* in 1845.

John and Caroline settled at **Willow Plains, near Clare**, where they farmed for **47 years**. They raised six sons:

1. [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]] (1875–1954) — Mark's great-grandfather
2. Ernest John Telfer (1878–1953)
3. William James Telfer (1880–?)
4. Albert George Telfer (1881–?)
5. Walter William Telfer (1884–1966)
6. Edwin Gilbert Telfer (1887–?)

John was described as a **prominent Clare resident** and was actively associated with every community move in the Willow Plains district. He was a **prominent member of the Methodist Church**, serving as **superintendent of the Sunday-school for about 30 years** (per both Advertiser and Chronicle obituaries).

### The Double Bereavement — 1929

In a remarkable and tragic turn, **John and Caroline died within hours of each other** in August 1929. John passed away on **23 August 1929** at age 82, and Caroline followed him **the next day**, 24 August 1929. The *Register News-Pictorial* ran a photo with the headline:

> "THE LATE MRS. JOHN TELFER, of Clare, who died within a few hours of her husband. Both were prominent Clare residents."

They were buried together at **Clare Cemetery**.

As the Advertiser obituary noted:
> "He was a resident of Willow Plains for 47 years. He was actively associated with every movement inaugurated for the wellbeing of the district, and was a prominent member of the Methodist Church and Sunday-school. Mr. Telfer held the position of superintendent of the Sunday-school for about 30 years."

Alan Dale Telfer was born on 27 October 1890 in Tantanoola, South Australia, the 13th child of John Telfer (1840–1913) and his second wife Martha Clara Henstridge.

He never married. During the Great Depression of the 1920s-1930s, Alan migrated far from the agricultural safety of South Australia's Limestone Coast to the interior of New South Wales. He found work as a **ganger** (railway labor foreman) and **coalminer** — a gruelling and highly itinerant profession that took him deep into the state's central-west.

Alan's fate was a long-standing mystery in the Telfer family tree. The resolution came via an NSW Government Gazette intestate estate notice, which confirmed:

> Alan Dale Telfer, late of **Wilga Tank, Girilambone**, in the State of New South Wales, died **intestate** on **13 September 1937**.

Girilambone and the associated Wilga Tank area was a remote railway siding and copper mining outpost in central-western New South Wales. His death there, without a will, paints a picture of a rugged, transient, and likely impoverished life in his final years — a stark contrast to the settled farming life of his Tantanoola siblings.

His exact burial location is unknown but likely in the Girilambone district.

## Life Summary

Caroline Edna Lawrie was born in 1890 in the Gilbert district of South Australia, the daughter of **Robert Dunlop Lawrie** and **Caroline Hosking**. Her father was a farmer in the Long Plains / Balaklava district.

She married **[[William Henry Parker (1893–1968)]]** on 29 March 1917 in South Australia. William Henry was a farmer from the Long Plains area, son of [[William Humphrey Parker (1850–1926)]] and [[Hannah Parker (1855–1948)]].

They had **five children**: Avis, Howard Lindsay, Sydney Hugh, William Humphrey, and **[[Shirley Edna Telfer (1929–2017)|Shirley Edna Parker]]** (your grandmother).

**Notable family connection:** Caroline's brother **Frank Lindsay Lawrie** (1886–1920) married **Sophia Parker** — William Henry's sister — creating a sibling swap between the Lawrie and Parker families.

Caroline died in 1957.

---

## The Lawrie Line

Robert Dunlop Lawrie was the son of **John Lawrie** and **Janet Lawrie** (per Geni records). The Lawrie name is Scottish in origin — likely from Ayrshire or Renfrewshire — though Robert's parents' origins are still being researched.
